claims.text: HfNbTaTiZr is typically a single-phase BCC high-entropy alloy.
A hybrid machine-learning model can integrate first-principles phonon data with electronic-transport calculations to predict HfNbTaTiZr thermal transport.
The proposed model can accurately separate the lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions of HfNbTaTiZr.
Variable defect and oxygen concentrations can be represented in DFT-derived phonon spectra.
Those phonon spectra capture mass fluctuations and force-constant variations caused by defects and oxygen in HfNbTaTiZr.
Electronic-transport calculations can explicitly include oxygen-scattering effects in HfNbTaTiZr.
Chemical disorder and oxygen impurities induce lattice distortions and variations in interatomic force constants.
The disorder- and oxygen-induced structural changes modulate phonon scattering and electronic relaxation.
Total thermal conductivity comprises electronic and lattice contributions.
Separately modeling phonons and electronic carriers avoids reliance on an oversimplified Debye treatment.
Oxygen impurity content changes electronic carrier relaxation times.
The proposed model will reduce total-thermal-conductivity prediction error by about 30% relative to previous approaches.
Predicted lattice and electronic thermal conductivities will each agree within approximately 10–15% of experiment over 200–1200 K.
Existing approaches for this problem use DFT-derived elastic properties, Debye-temperature estimates, and nearly perfect crystal models.
A prior transport approach estimates electronic thermal conductivity through the Wiedemann–Franz law with an approximated Lorenz number.
The proposed model is applicable to nominally pure and approximately 1 wt.% oxygen-containing HfNbTaTiZr under equilibrium bulk conditions from 200 to 1200 K.
Performance outside 200–1200 K or above approximately 1 wt.% oxygen is not established.
The magnitude of the improvement depends on the coverage and quality of the ab initio training data and on the accuracy of experimental separation of phonon and electronic contributions.
Low-temperature transport introduces added uncertainty because Wiedemann–Franz behavior can deviate below 300 K.
Electrical-conductivity and Lorenz-factor measurements can be used to estimate the electronic thermal-conductivity contribution.
